To pretermit something means to pass it over — to leave it out, skip it, or set it aside, whether deliberately or through neglect. Think of it as intentionally (or carelessly) stepping around something instead of engaging with it.

The "something" can be a topic you chose not to mention, a duty you failed to carry out, a question you deliberately set aside, or even a habit or practice you temporarily suspended.

This word carries a cluster of closely related meanings. Understanding all of them together gives you the full picture.

1. To omit or leave out — to not mention something
This is the simplest sense. If a writer pretermits a detail in their account, they leave it out — they don't mention it. The omission can be deliberate or the result of carelessness.

"The report pretermitted several key findings."
(The report simply left those findings out.)

2. To neglect a duty or fail to do something you should have done
Here, the word is about inaction — failing to perform a responsibility or obligation.

"He pretermitted his duties as a guardian."
(He failed to carry out his responsibilities.)

3. To deliberately set aside a question or issue — without forgetting it
This is the most nuanced and important sense, and the one most alive in modern usage. When you pretermit something in this sense, you are not forgetting it, and you are not avoiding it out of cowardice — you are consciously and deliberately choosing not to address it, usually for a specific, reasoned purpose.

This is exactly how the word is most commonly used today, particularly in legal writing. Courts frequently use "pretermit" when they deliberately decide not to rule on a particular legal issue — because the case can be resolved without needing to touch that issue.

"The court pretermits the constitutional question, as the matter is resolved on statutory grounds."
(The court is deliberately and consciously setting aside the constitutional question — not ignoring it carelessly, but making a principled, reasoned decision not to address it in this case.)

This legal usage is precise and important: it signals a reasoned, intentional act of non-engagement, not an oversight.

4. To interrupt or suspend a practice or custom
Less commonly, "pretermit" can mean to discontinue or temporarily suspend something that was ongoing — a habit, tradition, or regular practice.

"The annual ceremony was pretermitted during the years of conflict."
(The ceremony was suspended/discontinued for that period.)
The Most Important Nuance: Deliberate vs. Negligent

One thing that makes "pretermit" richer than a word like "omit" is that it can swing between intentional and unintentional omission. Context usually tells you which is meant:

  • In legal writing, pretermitting is almost always deliberate and reasoned — the court knows the issue is there and chooses not to rule on it.
  • In general writing, pretermitting can sometimes imply careless neglect — someone overlooked something they should have addressed.

This dual nature is part of why the word requires a little more attention than a simple synonym like "skip" or "omit."
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close neighbors, but they are not identical:

  • Omit is the most neutral, everyday equivalent — to leave something out. "Pretermit" is simply the formal, elevated version of this.
  • Overlook suggests accidental failure to notice — not always deliberate.
  • Neglect stresses a failure of duty through carelessness — it has a more negative moral weight.
  • Disregard means to intentionally pay no attention to something — it can carry a defiant tone.
  • Bypass implies going around an obstacle — it emphasizes the act of avoidance more than the omission itself.

"Pretermit" sits at the formal, precise end of this family. It can cover deliberate and negligent omission, and crucially, it doesn't necessarily carry the negative moral judgment that "neglect" does, nor the defiant tone of "disregard."
Register and Where You'll Encounter It

This is a formal, elevated word. You will almost never hear it in everyday speech. You are most likely to encounter it in:

  • Legal writing — court opinions, briefs, and judgments (this is its most active home today)
  • Formal academic or scholarly prose
  • Literary or archaic texts

If you see it in a court opinion, you can be confident it means the court is deliberately setting aside a legal question without ruling on it. In other formal contexts, it most likely means to leave out or omit — whether by choice or neglect.

If you had to carry one idea in your head about "pretermit," let it be this: to pass something over — to leave it unaddressed, unmentioned, or undone. The passage can be deliberate and reasoned (as in a court setting aside a legal question), or it can be a failure of duty (neglecting a responsibility). The word is always formal, always precise, and always signals that something which could have been addressed, wasn't.
